subject: Banking
title: Why Banks Love Checking Accounts
description: A 60-second lesson on Why Banks Love Checking Accounts.

hook.text: Checking accounts pay zero interest. Banks lend that money at 7%. Free deposits are the most profitable funding source.

buildup.text: Banks call non-interest-bearing deposits 'core deposits.' They're stable, free.

discovery.text: JPMorgan has $2.4 trillion in deposits. A large share paying zero interest generates billions in free lending capital.

twist.text: Banks spend heavily on free checking perks to attract these deposits.

climax.text: Free checking isn't charity. It's the cheapest funding a bank can get, and they would spend a lot to keep it.

punchline.text: Free checking pays the bank, not you. Zero-interest deposits are pure profit.

quiz.question: Why do banks offer free checking accounts?
options: Zero-interest deposits are the cheapest source of lending capital

details.summary: Checking accounts are the gateway product for banks because they provide cheap funding through deposits that earn near-zero interest, and they create sticky customer relationships that facilitate cross-selling of profitable loan and fee products.
details.whyItMatters: Banks compete aggressively for checking accounts because they represent the cheapest source of funding and the strongest customer relationship. A checking account customer is five times more likely to buy additional bank products.
takeaways: Checking deposits pay near-zero interest while the bank earns 4-5 percent lending them
Checking customers are five times more likely to buy additional products
Switching costs keep customers locked in despite better options elsewhere

faq.question: Why do banks offer free checking accounts?
faq.answer: Free checking attracts deposits that fund bank lending at near-zero cost. The bank earns the full interest rate on loans made with those deposits. Free checking also establishes the customer relationship that enables profitable cross-selling of credit cards, loans, and investments.

faq.question: Why is it so hard to switch checking accounts?
faq.answer: Direct deposits, automatic bill payments, and linked debit cards create high switching costs. Changing banks requires updating dozens of payment connections. Banks design this stickiness intentionally to retain customers and the cheap deposits they bring.
